questions.q: What problem does the lesson say an eval dataset solves?
options: It reduces the AI provider's hosting costs
It turns 'I think this still works' into something you can actually demonstrate consistently, instead of relying on informal, one-off testing
It automatically writes the application's code
It eliminates the need for a system prompt
questions.explain: The lesson frames eval datasets as the fix for 'vibes-based' testing that silently breaks when something changes.

questions.q: In the lesson's example eval dataset format, what two things does each test case pair together?
options: A username and a password
A realistic input and a way to judge whether the output was acceptable
A model name and its release date
A price and a currency code
questions.explain: The lesson's YAML example shows each entry pairing a 'vars' input with an 'assert' check for judging the output.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the single best source of eval test cases once a system is live?
options: Random text generators
Competitor marketing materials
A developer's personal guesses about what users might ask
Real production inputs, sampled and reviewed, because they reflect real phrasing and ambiguity
questions.explain: The lesson identifies real production inputs as the best source, since they capture real-world phrasing and edge cases a developer wouldn't think to write.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about dataset size — is bigger always better?
options: Datasets should never exceed 10 test cases total
Size doesn't matter at all for eval datasets
A well-curated, smaller dataset (e.g. 150 reviewed cases) beats a much larger but unreviewed one
Only datasets of exactly 1,000 cases are considered valid
questions.explain: The lesson states a well-curated 150 cases beats an unreviewed 5,000, emphasizing quality and review over raw volume.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a static eval dataset from launch day becomes a problem over time?
options: Because it stops reflecting reality within months if it isn't versioned and grown as production issues are found
Because old test cases automatically expire and delete themselves
Because static datasets cost more to store than dynamic ones
Because launch-day datasets are always too large
questions.explain: The lesson notes a dataset needs to be versioned and maintained, growing from logged failures, or it stops reflecting how the system is actually used.
